name: Yantsu
meaning: Usually written with characters read as 'safe three' and glossed in Kyokushin as 'to keep pure', striving to maintain integrity of principle under pressure; the etymology is debated.
origin_person: uncertain; plausibly adapted by Mas Oyama from the kata Ansan/Hansan of Motobu-ha Shito-ryu
provenance: The most origin-disputed kata in Kyokushin: style histories suggest descent from Ansan (Hansan) preserved in Motobu-ha Shito-ryu, modified by Oyama, but no primary documentation settles the question, so all accounts should be treated as provisional. It appears in no mainstream Okinawan syllabus outside these lines.

name: Anan
variants: Anan Dai (extended competition version); Annan; Ānan
meaning: Meaning uncertain: the characters can be read as 'peace in the south' and are often linked to Annan (a historical name for Vietnam) or to a Chinese place or personal name. Ryuei-ryu's most famous kata, noted for lateral evasion and techniques repeated no more than twice.
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
introduced_by: Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenko Nakaima (standardised); Teruo Hayashi (brought); Tsuguo Sakumoto (standardised)
provenance: Kept secret within the Nakaima family for four generations until Kenko Nakaima opened Ryuei-ryu in 1971; Teruo Hayashi carried it into Hayashi-ha Shito-ryu, and Tsuguo Sakumoto's WUKO world titles (1984-1988) made it a dominant competition kata. The family origin story (Norisato's c. 7 years with Ryu Ryu Ko in Fuzhou) is tradition with limited external corroboration.

name: Chikan
meaning: Earth (chi) form: third elemental kata of Kojo-ryu, grounding the zodiac kamae-te method in low, rooted positions.
era: imported in the 4th family generation (Kaho Kojo, 1849-1925)
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China / Kume village, Naha
provenance: Completes the heaven-void-earth set attributed to Kaho Kojo's importation from Fuzhou; like all Kojo-ryu material its history rests on family tradition rather than external records.

name: Gekisai dai ichi
variants: Gekisai (Fukyu) kata I; Geksai dai; Kyokushin: Gekisai dai
meaning: Attack and smash, number one. A deliberately simple popularisation kata: direct blocks, lunging punches and kicks designed to teach schoolchildren and beginners quickly.
provenance: Created in 1940 for the karate promotion committee convened under Okinawa governor Hayakawa Gen, as Naha-te's contribution to a common beginner syllabus alongside Shoshin Nagamine's Fukyugata ichi. Later absorbed into Kyokushin as Gekisai dai.

name: Gekisai dai ni
variants: Gekisai (Fukyu) kata II; Kyokushin: Gekisai sho
meaning: Attack and smash, number two. Extends Gekisai dai ichi with open-hand techniques, mawashi-uke and neko-ashi-dachi, introducing the softer receiving methods characteristic of Goju-ryu.
provenance: Companion kata to Gekisai dai ichi from the same 1940 popularisation programme; the pair are Miyagi's last compositions and the standard entry point of the modern Goju curriculum.

name: Hakkaku
variants: Hakkaku (white crane); distinct from the Matayoshi/Gokenki Hakkaku-Hakucho crane kata of the same name
meaning: White crane. Third and highest animal kata of Kojo-ryu, expressing evasive footwork and wing-like simultaneous deflection and strike.
era: undocumented; family tradition reaches back to the 18th century
origin_person: Kojo family tradition ascribes the animal kata to the lineage of Kojo Uekata (Cai Zhaogong)
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China
provenance: Completes the tiger-dragon-crane triad; extended Kojo-ryu lists also record Hafa, Nepai, Nunfa, Paichu and other Fujian-named forms, consistent with the family's Kume-village Chinese heritage but thinly documented. Kojo-ryu is grouped here with Naha-te as Kuninda-di for cladogram purposes. [Verifier: Exists; 'white crane', highest animal kata, correct in meaning and character. Same caveat: the Koj

name: Hakko
meaning: White tiger. First of Kojo-ryu's three advanced animal kata (tiger, dragon, crane), expressing hard crushing and clawing method.
era: undocumented; family tradition reaches back to the 18th century
origin_person: Kojo family tradition ascribes the animal kata to the lineage of Kojo Uekata (Cai Zhaogong)
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China
provenance: The three 'white beast' kata are the core of the family style; the attribution to the early Kojo generations (and their teacher-relations with Fuzhou masters such as Wai Shin Zan) is folklore preserved by the family, not independently documented. [Verifier: The kata exists and 'white tiger' is correct; Hakko, Hakuryu and Hakkaku are confirmed as Kojo-ryu's advanced animal triad. However, published

name: Hakuryu
meaning: White dragon. Second animal kata of Kojo-ryu, expressing soft, coiling, whipping method between the tiger's hardness and the crane's lightness.
era: undocumented; family tradition reaches back to the 18th century
origin_person: Kojo family tradition ascribes the animal kata to the lineage of Kojo Uekata (Cai Zhaogong)
origin_place: Kume village, Naha / Fuzhou, Fujian, China
provenance: Preserved through the Kojo family line (Isei, Taitei, Kaho, Saikyo, Kafu, Shigeru Kojo) and a handful of outside students; the pre-Okinawan history is family folklore. [Verifier: Exists; 'white dragon', second animal kata, correct. Same attribution caveat as Hakko: sources point to Kojo Taitei introducing the animal triad, so the 18th-century Kojo Uekata lineage claim is unverifiable tradition.]

name: Heiku
meaning: Black tiger. Sister kata to Paiku expressing the darker, heavier side of Fujian tiger boxing; the two share much material and are distinguished by rhythm and emphasis.
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
introduced_by: Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenko Nakaima (standardised); Teruo Hayashi (brought)
provenance: Nakaima family transmission opened to the public in 1971; entered mainstream competition through Hayashi-ha Shito-ryu and Sakumoto's students. Kanji renderings vary across sources as the names are phonetic Fujian dialect.

name: Kukan
meaning: Void or sky (ku) form: second of the three elemental kata of Kojo-ryu, continuing the zodiac kamae-te system at intermediate level.
era: imported in the 4th family generation (Kaho Kojo, 1849-1925)
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China / Kume village, Naha
provenance: Middle kata of the heaven-void-earth trio said to have been brought from the Kojo family dojo in Fuzhou by Kaho Kojo; preserved only in the nearly extinct Kojo-ryu line (Kafu Kojo, Shigeru Kojo, Hayashi Shingo).

name: Kururunfa
meaning: Conventionally 'holding on long and striking suddenly' (the kanji are phonetic). The most fluid of the classical Goju kata, alternating slow sticky-hand control with explosive release; strong White Crane character.
provenance: Goju tradition ascribes it to Higaonna via Ryu Ryu Ko, but it is absent from To'on-ryu and its documented history before Miyagi is thin; scholars regard the pre-Okinawan origin as unverified.

name: Nepai
variants: Neipai; Nijuhachi; Nipaipo (二十八歩, Mabuni's Shito-ryu adaptation)
meaning: Twenty-eight (steps). A Fujian Whooping/White Crane form built on fast whipping strikes and crane-wing deflections; in Okinawa it is the signature legacy of the Chinese tea merchant Gokenki.
provenance: Kyoda Juhatsu learned Nepai directly from Gokenki and fixed it in the To'on-ryu curriculum; Kenwa Mabuni reworked the same material as Nipaipo in Shito-ryu. A Nepai also appears in extended Kojo-ryu kata lists, consistent with the family's Kume-village White Crane contacts.

name: Niseishi (Ryuei-ryu)
variants: Niseshi; cognate with Aragaki Niseishi / Nijushiho but a distinct transmission
meaning: Twenty-four (steps/hands). The Ryuei-ryu version of a Fuzhou form also transmitted separately by Aragaki Seisho (whence Shito-ryu's Niseishi and Shotokan's Nijushiho).
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
provenance: Listed in the Ryuei-ryu (Ryuho-kai) curriculum alongside Sanchin, Seisan and Sanseiru; its coexistence with Seisho Arakaki's independent Niseishi line supports a shared Fuzhou source pool rather than a single Okinawan origin.

name: Ohan
meaning: Meaning and kanji uncertain (phonetic Fujian name; sometimes glossed as 'king's crown' or a personal name in style folklore). Alternates heavy rooted techniques with sudden turns and double-hand strikes.
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
provenance: Nakaima family kata made public in 1971; its extended version Ohan Dai became globally visible when Kiyou Shimizu and other Shito-ryu-trained competitors performed it at WKF finals and the Tokyo 2020 Olympics.

name: Pachu
variants: Pachu Dai/Sho in some competition listings; Pāchū
meaning: Meaning and kanji uncertain (a phonetic Fujian-dialect name). An extremely fast, dynamic kata teaching lateral evasion and moving into the opponent with difficult combinations.
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
introduced_by: Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenko Nakaima (standardised); Teruo Hayashi (brought)
provenance: One of the six kata unique to the Nakaima family line (Anan, Paiku, Heiku, Pachu, Ohan, Paiho), secret until 1971 and now on the WKF kata list; the untranslatable name reflects oral Fuzhou transmission.

name: Paiho
meaning: White phoenix (or white crane). A characteristic White Crane kata: light footwork, wing-like simultaneous deflection and strike; its opening closely parallels Hakkaku, Hakucho and other Okinawan crane forms from the Gokenki milieu.
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
provenance: The most explicitly crane-styled of the Nakaima family kata, kept within the family until Kenko Nakaima's 1971 opening of the school; rarely seen outside Ryuei-ryu organisations.

name: Paiku
meaning: White tiger. Embodies Fujian tiger-boxing method within the Nakaima family curriculum: clawing hands, pouncing shifts and hard direct power; paired conceptually with Heiku (black tiger).
era: Qing-era China; brought to Okinawa c. 1840s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
introduced_by: Norisato Nakaima (brought); Kenko Nakaima (standardised); Teruo Hayashi (brought)
provenance: Part of the Nakaima family transmission from Ryu Ryu Ko, made public by Kenko Nakaima in 1971 and adopted into Hayashi-ha Shito-ryu and WKF competition lists; very similar in structure to Heiku.

name: Saifa
meaning: Smash and tear (destroy and defeat). Teaches escaping from grabs at close quarters with whipping strikes, hammer-fists and tearing hand actions.
provenance: Traditionally credited to Higaonna's Fuzhou study under Ryu Ryu Ko, but its absence from Kyoda Juhatsu's To'on-ryu (which preserves only Sanchin, Sesan, Sanseru and Pechurin from Higaonna) leads scholars such as Mario McKenna to suggest Miyagi introduced it from his own Chinese research; treat the Higaonna attribution as tradition rather than documented fact.

name: Sanchin
variants: Sam Chien (Fujian saam chin); Sanchin dai ichi / dai ni (Goju); Uechi Sanchin
meaning: Three battles (or conflicts): the struggle to unify mind, body and breath. The foundational conditioning kata of all Naha-lineage karate, built on rooted stance, dynamic tension and controlled breathing.
era: Qing-era China; taught in Naha from c. 1880s
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted the Higaonna line; ultimate creator unknown, Fujian tradition)
introduced_by: Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Kanbun Uechi (brought)
provenance: Two independent transmissions from Fuzhou: Higaonna brought a version credited to Ryu Ryu Ko (said to have been performed with open hands, which Higaonna, or by some accounts Miyagi, closed into fists; Miyagi also removed the turns and slowed the breathing, creating the Goju version), while Kanbun Uechi brought Zhou Zihe's Pangai-noon version, which keeps open-hand nukite strikes and faster, unforced breathing. The identification of Ryu Ryu Ko with the Whooping Crane master Xie Zongxiang is plausible but disputed scholarship.

name: Sanseiru
meaning: Thirty-six (hands). The number is usually explained through Buddhist/Chinese numerology (6 x 6: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, spirit; colour, voice, taste, smell, touch, justice). Features low kicks, joint attacks and double-hand techniques.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
introduced_by: Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Norisato Nakaima (brought)
provenance: One of the four kata reliably traceable to Higaonna (preserved in both Goju-ryu and To'on-ryu). The Nakaima family's Ryuei-ryu preserves its own Sanseiru from the same Ryu Ryu Ko source, and Uechi-ryu's Sanseiryu (listed separately) is a distinct Pangai-noon form sharing only the name.

name: Seiyunchin
meaning: Usually rendered as 'to control and pull into battle' (the kanji are a phonetic gloss); sometimes 'calm within the storm'. A kick-free kata of grappling, unbalancing and pulling techniques performed largely in shiko-dachi.
provenance: Attributed by Goju tradition to Higaonna's Naha-te, though like Saifa it is absent from To'on-ryu, so a Miyagi-era introduction is possible. Entered Kyokushin (as Seienchin) via the Goju line, and Isshin-ryu (as Seiunchin) through Tatsuo Shimabuku's study under Miyagi.

name: Sepai
meaning: Eighteen (hands), conventionally 6 x 3 in Buddhist numerology (the six senses in three aspects). An advanced kata of angular evasion, hidden strikes and off-line body shifting.
provenance: Attributed by tradition to Higaonna's Fuzhou study; not preserved in To'on-ryu, so the same caveat as Saifa applies. Practised in Kyokushin as Seipai via the Goju-kai line.

name: Sesan
variants: Hangetsu and Shuri Seisan are cognate but distinct Shuri/Tomari forms; Seisan (Naha lineage); Sēsan
meaning: Thirteen (hands), variously explained as thirteen techniques or 13 as an auspicious number. The Naha version emphasises close-range hard-soft striking, low kicks and heavy rooted stepping.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
introduced_by: Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Juhatsu Kyoda (standardised); Norisato Nakaima (brought)
provenance: Seisan is arguably the most widely distributed kata name in karate; this entry covers the Naha transmission preserved in Goju-ryu, To'on-ryu (one of Kyoda's four Higaonna kata) and Ryuei-ryu. The Uechi and Shuri/Tomari Seisan are separate transmissions. [Verifier: Kata, meaning ('thirteen') and Naha character correct. The introduced_by set is defensible (Kyoda's To'on-ryu preserves Higaonna's Sesa

name: Shisochin
meaning: Battle in four directions. Combines nukite spear-hand attacks with joint-locking palm techniques delivered to all four compass points; said to have been Chojun Miyagi's favourite kata in later life.
provenance: Goju tradition places it among the kata Higaonna brought from Fuzhou; its absence from To'on-ryu again makes the transmission route uncertain and possibly Miyagi's own addition.

name: Suparinpei
variants: Bechurin; Hyakuhachiho; Pechurin (ペッチュウリン, To'on-ryu); Sūpārinpei
meaning: One hundred and eight (hands), the Buddhist number of worldly desires (bonno) dispelled at New Year; symbolises completeness. The longest and highest kata of the Goju curriculum, integrating the whole system.
origin_person: Ryu Ryu Ko (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
introduced_by: Kanryo Higaonna (brought); Chojun Miyagi (standardised); Juhatsu Kyoda (standardised)
provenance: One of the four Higaonna kata corroborated by both the Miyagi and Kyoda lines. Kyoda preserved it under the older name Pechurin ('one hundred continuous steps'), and the To'on-ryu version is regarded as closer to Higaonna's original than Miyagi's Suparinpei.

name: Tenkan
meaning: Heaven (ten) form: first of Kojo-ryu's three elemental kata (heaven, void, earth). Its opening kamae cycle encodes the twelve zodiac-animal guard postures (kamae-te) that define the style's fighting method.
era: imported in the 4th family generation (Kaho Kojo, 1849-1925)
origin_place: Fuzhou, Fujian, China / Kume village, Naha
provenance: Kojo-ryu (Kuninda-di) was transmitted privately within the Kojo family of Kume village, descendants of Cai Zhaogong (Kojo Uekata); family tradition says Kaho Kojo imported the three elemental kata from the family's Fuzhou dojo. Documentation is sparse and rests on family testimony reported by researchers such as Mario McKenna.

name: Tensho
meaning: Rotating (turning) palms. The soft (ju) counterpart to Sanchin's hardness: flowing open-hand blocks and strikes on a Sanchin base, embodying the go-ju polarity that names the style.
provenance: Composed by Miyagi in 1921 from breathing and palm-change patterns he associated with the Rokkishu (six hands) of Fujian White Crane, reportedly informed by his 1915 research trip to Fuzhou. Adopted into Kyokushin via Mas Oyama's Goju training under Gogen Yamaguchi and So Nei Chu.

name: Ananku
variants: Anaku; Ananko; Anankū; Annanko; Annanku; Ānankū
meaning: Commonly glossed 'peace from the south' or 'light from the south', usually connected with Annam (Vietnam) or with Kyan's 1930s trip south to Taiwan; a short, direct kata built largely from Kyan's other forms.
era: c. 1930s (some accounts say as early as 1895)
provenance: The youngest kata in the traditional Shōrin repertoire: most accounts (including Nagamine's) say Kyan composed it, or adapted a form he saw, after visiting Taiwan around 1930-1931. It passed to his students' styles (Matsubayashi-ryū, Seibukan, Shobayashi, Shōrinji-ryū) and, as Anaku, into Trias's Shuri-ryū.

name: Channan
variants: Chan Nan; Chiang Nan; Shiraguma/Shiro Kuma identification (per Iwai Tsukuo)
meaning: Meaning unknown; suggested to be a Chinese personal or place name (sometimes rendered Chiang Nan). Significant as the proto-Pinan: the working name or source form from which Itosu built the Pinan series.
origin_person: Anko Itosu (as recorded; possibly reworking older Chinese material)
provenance: Known chiefly from Motobu Chōki's testimony that Itosu first called his new school kata Channan before settling on Pinan; the original form is lost, and later 'Channan' reconstructions are modern. Iwai Tsukuo (a student of Motobu Chōsei) claimed in 1997 that Motobu's Shiraguma kata preserved the old Channan; this is unverified and should be treated as folklore.

name: Chatan Yara no Kusanku
variants: Chatan Yara Kushanku; Chatanyara Kusanku; Yara Kusanku
meaning: 'Kusanku of Yara of Chatan village': the longest Kusanku version, attributed to Chatan Yara, said to have studied in China; prized for its wide, flowing movement and now a celebrated tournament kata.
provenance: The attribution to Chatan Yara (1668-1756) is traditional and partly folkloric; the version reached the modern era through Chōtoku Kyan's line (Kyan reportedly learned it from Yara of Chatan's descendants) and so entered Seibukan, Shobayashi, Shōrinji-ryū and Isshin-ryū, and Shitō-ryū via Hayashi-ha. It became world famous through WKF competition.

name: Chinte
meaning: 珍手, 'rare/unusual hands', after its uncommon techniques (two-finger strikes, circular arm blows); often noted as containing methods suited to smaller or female practitioners.
provenance: Of unknown, strongly Chinese-flavoured origin, transmitted through the Itosu curriculum to Mabuni and Funakoshi; Funakoshi's attempted renaming Shōin did not stick and the kata survives as Chinte in Shotokan and Shitō-ryū, including its curious backward-hopping ending.

name: Chinto
variants: Chintō; Gankaku (岩鶴); Jin Do / Chinto (진도, Korean)
meaning: Traditionally the name of a shipwrecked Chinese sailor (folklore) from whom the kata's techniques were learned; the kanji 鎮東 can be read 'settling the east'. Funakoshi's Gankaku (岩鶴) means 'crane on a rock', after the signature one-legged stance.
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (standardised); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: Folklore holds that a castaway Chinese sailor called Chintō taught the material near Tomari; parallel Shuri (Matsumura/Itosu) and Tomari (Matsumora, thence Kyan) versions descend from it, which is why Shotokan's differs from the Kyan-line versions in Isshin-ryū and Matsubayashi-ryū. Funakoshi renamed it Gankaku in the mid-1930s.

name: Gojushiho
variants: Gojushiho Dai / Gojushiho Sho (Shotokan); Gojūshiho; Hotaku (Funakoshi's short-lived renaming); O Sip Sa Bo (Korean); Useishi (ウーセーシー, Okinawan for 54)
meaning: 'Fifty-four steps', a number of Buddhist significance in Chinese boxing (Useishi is the Okinawan reading of 54). An advanced 'drunken'-flavoured kata regarded as one of the highest in the Shuri repertoire.
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (standardised); Anko Itosu (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: Transmitted in the Matsumura-Itosu line (older Okinawan lines keep the name Useishi); Itosu's reworking yielded the versions from which Shotokan derives Gojūshiho Dai and Shō. Funakoshi initially renamed it Hōtaku ('woodpecker', after its pecking hand strikes) in the 1930s, but the original name prevailed.

name: Hakutsuru
variants: Hakutsuru no kata; Matsumura Hakutsuru; White Crane
meaning: 白鶴, 'white crane': embodies Fujian White Crane principles (one-legged crane stances, whipping open-hand strikes, soft-hard breathing) said to be the hidden essence of the Matsumura family art.
era: claimed mid-19th century; made public mid-20th century
origin_place: attributed to Fuzhou, Fujian, China / Shuri, Okinawa
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (created); Nabe Matsumura (standardised); Hohan Soken (brought)
provenance: Tradition in Matsumura Seito holds that Sōkon Matsumura learned White Crane material in China and kept the kata as a family secret, passed to his grandson Nabe Matsumura and then to Hōhan Sōken, who first showed it publicly after returning to Okinawa in the 1950s. Independent documentation before Sōken is lacking, so the pre-20th-century pedigree should be treated as family tradition/folklore. [Ve

name: Jiin
variants: Ji'in; Jion group third kata; Shōkyō (松柏, Funakoshi's short-lived renaming)
meaning: Usually glossed 'temple grounds' or 'mercy and shadow' (the kanji are unsettled); third member of the Jion group, sharing its salutation kamae.
provenance: Transmitted with Jion and Jitte through the Itosu line; Funakoshi's attempted renaming Shōkyō did not take hold, and the kata was later dropped from the JKA Shotokan examination syllabus though it survives in Shitō-ryū and some Shotokan lineages.

name: Jitte
meaning: 十手, 'ten hands': traditionally explained as fighting with the strength or effectiveness of ten men; contains movements interpreted as defences against the bō.
provenance: Second kata of the Jion group, of unknown origin, transmitted through Itosu to Funakoshi and Mabuni; practised in Shotokan, Shitō-ryū and Wadō-ryū with the original name retained.

name: Juroku
meaning: 十六, 'sixteen': widely said to commemorate the year of its creation, Shōwa 16 (1941); a compact intermediate kata built on Itosu-line (Shuri) movement principles.
provenance: Created by Mabuni in Osaka as a teaching kata within his Itosu-kei (Shuri-line) grouping of Shitō-ryū; now standard across most Shitō-ryū branches and seen in WKF competition.

name: Kusanku
native: 公相君 / クーサンクー
variants: Kanku Dai (観空大); Kong Sang Koon (공상군); Koshokun; Kosokun; Kusanku Dai; Kushanku; Kūsankū
meaning: Named after Kūsankū (Kwang Shang Fu), a Chinese envoy/military attaché who visited Okinawa around 1756. Funakoshi's renaming Kankū (観空) means 'to view the sky', after the opening gesture; the kata is regarded as the pinnacle of the Shuri-te repertoire and the ancestor of the Pinan series.
origin_person: Kanga Sakukawa (attributed), after the envoy Kūsankū
introduced_by: Kusanku (brought); Kanga Sakukawa (created); Anko Itosu (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: Tradition (partly folklore, anchored by the 1762 Ōshima Hikki record of a Chinese called Kūsankū demonstrating grappling in Okinawa) holds that Sakugawa composed the kata after studying with the envoy; it passed through Matsumura and Itosu, who standardised the Dai version. Funakoshi renamed it Kankū Dai in the mid-1930s (Karate-dō Kyōhan, 1935); the Korean Kong Sang Koon of Tang Soo Do preserves the Okinawan name.

name: Kusanku Sho
variants: Kanku Sho; Kosokun Sho; Kūsankū Shō
meaning: 'Lesser Kusanku': Itosu's second, more compact arrangement of the Kusanku material, named after the envoy Kūsankū; Kankū Shō ('to view the sky, minor') is the Shotokan reading.
provenance: Itosu reworked the old Kusanku into Dai and Shō versions for systematic teaching; Funakoshi renamed the pair Kankū Dai and Kankū Shō in the mid-1930s. Practised today mainly in Kobayashi Shōrin-ryū, Shitō-ryū and Shotokan.

name: Matsumura no Passai
meaning: The Passai version attributed to Sōkon Matsumura, regarded as closer to the older Chinese-flavoured form than Itosu's school version; same 'breach a fortress' gloss.
provenance: Preserved in the Matsumura family line to Nabe Matsumura and Hōhan Sōken (Matsumura Seito), and separately recorded by Kenwa Mabuni in Shitō-ryū as Matsumura no Passai; in Chibana's Kobayashi line the Passai Dai is likewise credited to Matsumura, with Itosu's as Passai Shō.

name: Myojo
meaning: 明星, 'morning star (Venus)': a junior training kata whose name evokes guidance and aspiration for beginning students.
provenance: A rarer Mabuni-created basic kata, preserved mainly in the Mabuni family (Seitō Shitō-ryū) line alongside Shinsei and Jūroku; documentation is thinner than for his better-known creations.

name: Naihanchi
variants: Chulgi (철기); Naifanchi; Naifanchin; Naihanchi Shodan/Nidan/Sandan; Naihanji / Nae Bo Jin (Korean); Tekki 1-3
meaning: Etymology obscure: commonly glossed 'internal divided conflict' or explained by the sideways straddle stance (naihanchi-dachi) and lateral embusen, interpreted as fighting with one's back to a wall or on a paddy-field dyke. Funakoshi's Tekki (鉄騎) means 'iron horseman'. It was the foundation kata of old Shuri-te and Tomari-te.
era: 19th century or earlier; Nidan and Sandan c. 1900
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (standardised); Anko Itosu (created); Choki Motobu (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: The original (Shodan) predates Itosu, who reworked it and is generally credited with composing Nidan and Sandan; before the Pinan it was the first kata taught in Shuri and Tomari, and Chōki Motobu famously held that Naihanchi contained everything needed for fighting. Funakoshi renamed the three Tekki Shodan-Sandan in the mid-1930s; Korean lineages kept it as Naihanji/Chulgi.

name: Nidanbu
meaning: Roughly 'second-level martial (exercise)'; a linking or 'bridge' kata created to connect the principles of KishimotoDi's three koryu kata (Tachimura no Naihanchi, Passai and Kusanku) into one progression.
introduced_by: Soko Kishimoto (created); Seitoku Higa (brought); Kiyohiko Higa (standardised)
provenance: Unique to KishimotoDi: developed by Kishimoto Soko as a pedagogical aid between the old kata of the Tachimura line, and preserved through Higa Seitoku's Bugeikan. One of the few named kata creations attributable to the KishimotoDi lineage itself.

name: Niseishi
variants: E Sip Sa Bo (Korean); Nijūshiho; Niseishi Dai
meaning: 'Twenty-four (steps)': Niseishi is the Okinawan reading of 24, rendered in Japanese as Nijūshiho (二十四歩, 'twenty-four steps'), a numerological name typical of Chinese-derived kata.
introduced_by: Seisho Arakaki (created); Kenwa Mabuni (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: From Aragaki Seishō's line (Aragaki demonstrated related material at the 1867 reception for the last Chinese investiture mission); it reached Funakoshi via Mabuni/Aragaki students and was renamed Nijūshiho in Shotokan in the mid-1930s, while Wadō-ryū and Shitō-ryū keep Niseishi. It is also a core kata of Genseiryū.

name: Passai
variants: Bal Sae / Bassai (Korean); Bassai; Bassai Dai (抜塞大); Itosu no Passai; Passai Dai; Patsai
meaning: Original meaning obscure; the kanji 抜塞 adopted in Japan are read 'to extract/breach a fortress', often glossed 'to storm a fortress'. Theories link it to Chinese leopard-and-lion boxing; it is a core intermediate-advanced kata of every Shuri-descended style.
era: by the mid-19th century; origins unknown
origin_place: Okinawa (Shuri and Tomari transmissions; ultimate Chinese origin presumed)
provenance: Passai circulated in parallel Shuri and Tomari lines (Matsumura no Passai, Oyadomari no Passai of Tomari, Matsumora's version); Itosu standardised the Dai form taught in schools, and Funakoshi fixed the kanji/reading Bassai in the mid-1930s. The Tomari (Oyadomari/Matsumora) versions are covered under the Tomari-te lineage; Korean Tang Soo Do preserves it as Bassai.

name: Passai Sho
variants: Bassai Shō; Itosu no Passai Sho
meaning: 'Lesser Passai': Itosu's shorter companion form to Passai Dai, opening against a bō attack; same contested 'breach a fortress' gloss as the parent kata.
provenance: Created by Itosu as the Shō pair to the standardised Passai Dai; transmitted to Shotokan (as Bassai Shō, renamed by Funakoshi mid-1930s), Shitō-ryū and Kobayashi Shōrin-ryū.

name: Pinan
variants: Heian Shodan-Godan; Pinan Nidan-Shodan order swap in Shotokan; Pinan Shodan-Godan (I-V); Pyung Ahn / Pyong-an (평안)
meaning: 平安, 'peaceful and safe' (Okinawan/Chinese reading Pinan; Sino-Japanese Heian): Itosu reportedly chose the name to express that one who masters the series can be confident of protecting themselves. A five-kata pedagogical series distilled mainly from Kusanku (and, per tradition, the lost Channan) for schoolchildren.
provenance: Itosu created the series around 1904-1907 as an entry curriculum when karate entered Okinawan schools; Motobu Chōki recalled Itosu initially calling the material Channan. Funakoshi renamed them Heian in the mid-1930s and swapped the order of the first two; Korean kwan lineages transmit them as Pyung Ahn.

name: Rohai Shodan, Nidan, Sandan
native: 鷺牌 初段・二段・三段
variants: Itosu Rohai; Itosu no Rohai; Meikyo (Shotokan); Rohai Jo/Chu/Ge
meaning: 'Heron sign' in three graded versions; Itosu expanded the single Tomari Rohai into a pedagogical series, as he did with Pinan and Naihanchi. Funakoshi's Shotokan derivative was renamed Meikyo, 'bright (polished) mirror'.
introduced_by: Anko Itosu (created); Kenwa Mabuni (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: Itosu reworked the Matsumora/Tomari Rohai into shodan, nidan and sandan versions for school instruction; Mabuni preserved all three in Shito-ryu, Wado-ryu retains a single Rohai from the same material, and Funakoshi blended the series into the Shotokan kata Meikyo. Listed here rather than under Shuri-te because it is the direct cross-line offspring of the Tomari kata.

name: Seisan
variants: Ban Wol; Hangetsu; Hangetsu (半月); Matsumura no Seisan; Seisan; Seisan (Naha/Uechi versions are distinct); Seishan; Sesan
meaning: 十三, 'thirteen' (variously explained as thirteen techniques, modes or steps); one of the oldest kata names in Okinawa. Funakoshi's Hangetsu (半月) means 'half moon', after its crescent stepping and stance.
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa (Chinese antecedent; parallel Naha-te transmission)
introduced_by: Sokon Matsumura (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: This entry covers the Shuri (Matsumura no) Seisan, transmitted via Matsumura and popularised through Kyan's students (it is the first kata of Isshin-ryū and central in Seibukan and Shōrinji-ryū); Funakoshi renamed his version Hangetsu in the mid-1930s and Wadō-ryū keeps Seishan. The unrelated-in-transmission Naha-te/Uechi-ryū Seisan descends separately from Fujian boxing.

name: Shiho Kusanku
meaning: 四方, 'four directions' + Kusanku: a rare Itosu-attributed variant that redistributes Kusanku material along a four-directional embusen.
provenance: Attributed to Itosu's late reworkings of the Kusanku theme and preserved almost solely through Mabuni's Shitō-ryū and its branches (notably Itosu-kai/Itosu-ryū); the attribution rests on Shitō-ryū tradition rather than contemporary documents. [Verifier: Real kata (Shiho Kosokun), practised essentially only in Shito-ryu, redistributing Kusanku material in four directions. Attribution is contested:

name: Shinpa
meaning: Usually written 心波, 'mind wave' (also glossed 'new wave'): a rare Mabuni kata combining Shuri-line footwork with soft, wave-like hand actions often linked to his study of White Crane-influenced material.
provenance: Among the rarest of Mabuni's compositions, transmitted only in a few Shitō-ryū branches (notably the Mabuni family line); some accounts say it condenses material Mabuni learned from Gokenki and other Chinese sources, which remains unverified. [Verifier: Real rare Mabuni kata, but details are off: sources date it to 1925, inspired by Mabuni's meeting with Uechi Kanbun and the Uechi-ryu (Pangai-noon

name: Shinsei
variants: Shinsei Dai Ichi; Shinsei Dai Ichi / Dai Ni (some branches); Shinsei Dai Ni
meaning: 新生, 'new life/rebirth': an introductory kata created to give beginners the fundamental Shuri-line stances, blocks and strikes in a short sequence.
provenance: One of Mabuni's pedagogical creations for his Osaka curriculum (roughly parallel in purpose to Okinawa's contemporaneous Fukyūgata project); retained mainly in family-line and Kuniba-line Shitō-ryū branches. A separate Gōjū-line beginner kata of the same name exists, so attribution should be checked per branch.

name: Shiro Kuma
variants: Shiraguma; Shiraguma no kata; White Bear
meaning: 白熊, 'white bear' (polar bear): reportedly a short, direct fighting kata reflecting Motobu Chōki's pressure-tested, close-range kumite method.
provenance: A poorly documented kata attributed to Motobu Chōki, kept privately within the Motobu-ryū/Motobu Kenpō lineage and not shown publicly; Iwai Tsukuo (student of Motobu Chōsei) claimed in a 1997 letter that Shiraguma preserves Itosu's lost Channan. Both the attribution and the Channan identification are unverifiable and should be treated as lineage tradition. [Verifier: Attested: Motobu Choki is repo

name: Sochin
variants: Aragaki no Sochin; Hakko (Funakoshi's short-lived renaming); Sōchin
meaning: 壮鎮, commonly glossed 'tranquil force', 'grand suppression' or 'to move into calm'; in Shotokan it is defined by the rooted sōchin-dachi stance and an immovable, imperturbable character.
introduced_by: Seisho Arakaki (created); Kenwa Mabuni (standardised); Gigo Funakoshi (standardised)
provenance: The older version descends from Aragaki Seishō of Kume (a Chinese-language official whose kata entered Shuri-descended Japanese styles chiefly via Mabuni's Shitō-ryū). The Shotokan Sōchin is a substantial 1930s reworking attributed to Gigō (Yoshitaka) Funakoshi; Funakoshi's proposed renaming Hakkō did not survive.

name: Sunsu
meaning: Usually explained as 'strong man', said to be Shimabuku Tatsuo's nickname; an alternative account renders it 'son of the old man'. Its significance is as the signature kata of Isshin-ryu, a composite distilling techniques Shimabuku valued from the style's other seven empty-hand kata.
provenance: The only kata original to Isshin-ryu: Shimabuku, a student of Kyan, Motobu and Miyagi, assembled Sunsu from Shorin and Goju elements while formalising Isshin-ryu (named 1956), and it remains exclusive to the style. The translation of the name is disputed within the Isshin-ryu community.

name: Tachimura no Kusanku
native: タチムラのクーサンクー
meaning: The Kusanku (named after the Chinese envoy Kūsankū) of the Tachimura/KishimotoDi lineage; the second of the system's two advanced koryu kata, only recently permitted to be shared publicly in its correct form.
introduced_by: Kusanku (brought); Tachimura no Peichin (standardised); Soko Kishimoto (brought); Kiyohiko Higa (standardised)
provenance: KishimotoDi claims descent from Sakugawa, who by tradition learned from the envoy Kusanku himself, making this line's Kusanku a sibling of the Chatan Yara and Itosu versions; the claim beyond Tachimura is oral tradition. Preserved in the Bugeikan under Higa Kiyohiko and documented abroad by Ulf Karlsson and Noah Legel.

name: Tachimura no Naihanchi
native: タチムラのナイファンチ
meaning: The Naihanchi of the Tachimura lineage; the name Naihanchi has no settled translation ('sideways fighting' is conventional). Its significance is as the core kata of KishimotoDi, performed with distinctive whole-body koshi mechanics and flowing weight transfer unlike the Itosu versions.
introduced_by: Tachimura no Peichin (standardised); Soko Kishimoto (brought); Seitoku Higa (brought); Kiyohiko Higa (standardised)
provenance: KishimotoDi tradition traces the kata from 'Tode' Sakugawa through Bushi Tachimura no Peichin (1814-1899) to Kishimoto Soko (dates given variously 1862- or 1866-1945), who taught Higa Seitoku, founder of the Bugeikan, where his son Higa Kiyohiko heads the line today; Ulf Karlsson and Noah Legel have documented and spread it abroad. The pre-Kishimoto lineage rests on oral tradition.

name: Tachimura no Passai
meaning: The Passai ('breach a fortress', etymology uncertain) of the Tachimura/KishimotoDi lineage; one of the system's two advanced koryu kata, historically withheld and not generally shown publicly in complete form.
introduced_by: Tachimura no Peichin (standardised); Soko Kishimoto (brought); Seitoku Higa (brought); Kiyohiko Higa (standardised)
provenance: Transmitted Tachimura to Kishimoto Soko to Higa Seitoku (Bugeikan) to Higa Kiyohiko; KishimotoDi's guarded teaching culture means only partial public versions circulated until recently. Independent of both the Tomari and Itosu Passai lines, though ultimately part of the same Passai family.

name: Unsu
meaning: 雲手, 'cloud hands', usually explained by the opening in which the hands part like clouds, or as parting the clouds ('hands in the clouds'); an advanced kata famed in Shotokan for its jumping rotation.
provenance: Attributed to Aragaki Seishō's Chinese-derived teaching line; Mabuni preserved the older form in Shitō-ryū, while the Shotokan version (probably reshaped in the 1930s by Funakoshi's circle, with Gigō usually credited) diverged considerably and became a premier competition kata.

name: Kasshindi (Ichi, Ni, San)
native: 活心手（カッシンディー）
meaning: Rendered 'battle hand' (also glossed 'living-spirit hand'); a set of three kata expressing Motobu Udundi's combative applications, bridging the basic Motode kata and the school's tuiti and weapons work.
provenance: Created by Uehara Seikichi when he systematised Motobu Udundi's curriculum in the 20th century, alongside his standardisation of the material inherited from Motobu Choyu. Practised today under Motobu Chosei's Motobu-ryu organisation. name: Mekata (Anji-kata no Mekata)
native: 按司方の舞方（メーカタ）
variants: Anji-kata nu Mēkata; Dancing form of the lords; Mai no Ti; Mēkata
meaning: 'Dance form(s)': martial technique embedded in Ryukyuan dance, attributed to the anji (territorial lords) and palace ('udun-di/goten-te') tradition; Anji-kata no Mekata is glossed 'dancing form of the lords'. Significant as the claimed aristocratic, pre-karate stratum of Okinawan ti.
era: claimed Ryukyu Kingdom era; documented 20th century
introduced_by: Choyu Motobu (brought); Seikichi Uehara (standardised); Seitoku Higa (standardised)
provenance: Motobu Udundi preserves mekata as dance-embedded fighting method used with tuiti, and Higa Seitoku's Bugeikan likewise collected palace-hand and dance-form material alongside KishimotoDi; these, with the Tachimura line, are the main documented claimants to an 'anji/palace hand' tradition. name: Motode Ichi and Ni
native: 元手 一・二（ムトゥディー）
meaning: 'Basic (original) hand'; the two foundational kata of Motobu Udundi, described as 'Shuri sanchin', with Motode Ichi performed open-handed and Motode Ni with closed fists. They encode the upright, flowing body method underlying the school's tuiti grappling.
era: formalised 20th century; tradition claims 17th-century palace roots
provenance: Motobu Udundi, the hereditary art of the Motobu Udun descended from Motobu Chohei (17th century), was passed by Motobu Choyu to Uehara Seikichi, who standardised the curriculum and later returned the headship to Motobu Chosei (2003); the claim of unbroken palace transmission is family tradition, partly folklore. The Motode pair are its only conventional empty-hand kata. [Verifier: All substantive

name: Rinkan
meaning: A rare Tomari-te kata whose name has no reliably documented translation; described by Tokashiki Iken as one of the 'pure Tomari' kata alongside Wankan, Wanshu Dai/Sho and Rohai.
provenance: Known almost solely through the Gohakukai: Tokashiki Iken records it from his teacher Nakasone Seiyu without an earlier named source, so its pre-Nakasone history is undocumented. Preserved today within Tokashiki's Goju-ryu Tomari-te Karate-do Kyokai (Gohakukai). [Verifier: The kata is real and rare: Tokashiki Iken's list of pure Tomari kata (Wankan, Wanshu Sho/Dai, Rohai, Rinkan) is verified nearl

name: Tomari Chinto
variants: Chinto; Chintō; Gankaku (Shotokan renaming of the Itosu line); Tomari no Chinto
meaning: Named after Chintō, said to be a shipwrecked Chinese sailor who taught in exchange for shelter; the name has no standard translation. Its significance lies in the one-legged crane stances and turning techniques, which led Funakoshi to rename the parallel Itosu version Gankaku ('crane on a rock').
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (brought); Shoshin Nagamine (standardised); Tatsuo Shimabuku (standardised)
provenance: The Chintō castaway story is folklore with Shuri (Matsumura) and Tomari (Matsumora/Gusukuma) tellings; the Tomari line ran Matsumora to Iha Kodatsu (Gohakukai) and Matsumora to Kyan, whose angled-embusen version passed into Matsubayashi-ryu, Seibukan, Shorinji-ryu and, via Shimabuku, Isshin-ryu. The Itosu/Shuri Chinto (Shotokan Gankaku) is a parallel line covered under Shuri-te.

name: Tomari Kusanku
meaning: The Tomari transmission of Kusanku, named after the 18th-century Chinese envoy Kūsankū (Kong Sang Kun); distinct in pattern from the Chatan Yara and Itosu (Dai/Sho) versions. Significant as evidence that the Kusanku tradition entered Tomari independently of Shuri.
introduced_by: Kusanku (brought); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (brought); Tokashiki Iken (standardised)
provenance: Documented by Tokashiki Iken as one of the nine Gohakukai Tomari kata, transmitted Matsumora to Iha Kodatsu to Nakasone Seiyu; the attribution to the envoy Kusanku himself is traditional folklore. The mainstream Kusanku/Kanku family (Chatan Yara, Itosu, Kyan lines) is covered under Shuri-te.

name: Tomari Naihanchi
variants: Naifanchi (Tomari-di); Naifanchi I-III (Gohakukai); Tomari no Naifanchi
meaning: The Tomari transmission of Naihanchi ('sideways fighting'; etymology obscure), performed on a lateral embusen; in Tomari usage it was the mainstream foundation kata, existing in many versions, rather than an import from Shuri.
introduced_by: Karyu Uku (brought); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Tokashiki Iken (standardised)
provenance: Gohakukai research records Uku Karyu (c. 1800-1850) teaching Naihanchi to Matsumora Kosaku, with the line preserved through Iha Kodatsu and Nakasone Seiyu to Tokashiki Iken (Naifanchi I-III). Motobu Choki, who trained under Matsumora, made Naihanchi the core of his teaching, so the Motobu-ryu version carries Tomari influence; the Shuri/Itosu Naihanchi series is treated separately.

name: Tomari Passai
variants: Bassai; Matsumora no Passai; Oyadomari no Passai; Passai; Tomari Bassai; Tomari no Passai
meaning: Usually rendered 'to breach (or extract from) a fortress'; the etymology is uncertain. Signifies penetrating an opponent's defence, with characteristic light, shifting footwork that distinguishes the Tomari versions from the heavier Shuri (Matsumura/Itosu) Passai line.
introduced_by: Kishin Teruya (brought); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kokan Oyadomari (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (brought)
provenance: Gohakukai tradition records Teruya Kishin (1804-1864) teaching Passai to both Matsumora Kosaku and Oyadomari Kokan, producing the two Tomari lines (Matsumora no Passai, Oyadomari no Passai); a folklore variant says a shipwrecked Chinese taught it in Tomari. Kyan learned the Oyadomari version and spread it through his students (Matsubayashi-ryu, Seibukan, Shorinji-ryu); Mabuni preserved several Tomari versions in Shito-ryu, while the better-known Shuri Passai Dai/Sho line is treated separately.

name: Tomari Rohai
variants: Matsumora Rohai; Matsumora no Rohai; Rohai; Rōhai
meaning: 'Vision (or sign) of the heron', from the one-legged heron/crane stance that is its signature posture. The Tomari original is the model from which Itosu built his three Rohai and Funakoshi's Meikyo ultimately derives.
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (brought); Shoshin Nagamine (standardised)
provenance: Transmitted from Matsumora Kosaku to Iha Kodatsu, whose students carried it into Matsubayashi-ryu (Nagamine's Rohai) and to Nakasone Seiyu, from whom Tokashiki Iken preserved it in the Gohakukai; Shito-ryu keeps it as Matsumora Rohai alongside Itosu's three derivatives. Ultimate origin undocumented.

name: Wando
meaning: Name of uncertain meaning, possibly a personal name on the pattern of Wanshū; no reliable translation is documented. Cited as one of the rare kata of the Tomari tradition.
provenance: Marginally documented: Wando appears in some Japanese lists of Tomari-te kata and is taught as 'Tomari Wando' in Patrick McCarthy's Koryu Uchinadi curriculum, but it is not among the nine kata Tokashiki Iken documented for the Gohakukai, and the common attribution to the Matsumora line cannot be independently verified; treat the transmission history as partly folklore. name: Wankan
meaning: 'King's crown', suggesting a courtly or royal association within the Tomari tradition; the Shito-ryu line practises it as Matsukaze, 'pine-tree wind'. In Matsubayashi-ryu it is prized as a compact, combative kata of the Matsumora line.
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Kodatsu Iha (brought); Shoshin Nagamine (standardised); Kenwa Mabuni (renamed)
provenance: Transmitted Matsumora to Iha Kodatsu and preserved in the Gohakukai and Matsubayashi-ryu; the Shito-ryu line renamed it Matsukaze, and the short Shotokan Wankan, of debated provenance, is usually linked to Yoshitaka (Gigo) Funakoshi's late-1930s curriculum work. Ultimate origin undocumented.

name: Wanshu
variants: Anshu; Empi; Enpi (Shotokan); Wanshū Dai; Wanshū Shō; Wansu; Wansū
meaning: Traditionally named after Wanshū (Wang Ji), the 1683 Qing sappushi (investiture envoy) credited by folklore with teaching quanfa in Tomari; the name is a personal name, not a phrase. Funakoshi renamed the Itosu-line version Empi, 'flying swallow', after its darting rise-and-fall movement; the kata is also known for its hidden-fist strike and signature dumping throw.
introduced_by: Kishin Teruya (brought); Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Maeda Pechin (brought); Chotoku Kyan (brought); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: Gohakukai records two Tomari versions: Wansu Dai (Teruya Kishin to Matsumora) and Wansu Sho (Oyadomari line via Heianzan Ryozen); Kyan learned Wanshu from Maeda Pechin of Tomari and passed it to Matsubayashi-ryu, Seibukan, Shorinji-ryu and, via Shimabuku, Isshin-ryu. The Itosu/Shuri redaction reached Shotokan, where Funakoshi (with Gigo's revisions) published it as Empi in the 1930s; the 1683 envoy attribution is folklore.

name: Wansu
variants: Empi / Enpi (燕飛); Wang Shu; Wanshū; Wansū
meaning: Traditionally named after Wang Ji (Wanshū), a Chinese sappūshi envoy said to have visited Tomari in 1683 (folklore); Funakoshi's Empi (燕飛) means 'flight of the swallow', after its darting rising-and-dropping movement.
era: folklore places the source visit in 1683; kata documented from the 19th century
introduced_by: Kosaku Matsumora (standardised); Chotoku Kyan (standardised); Gichin Funakoshi (renamed)
provenance: A Tomari-te kata in origin, listed here for its Shuri-line transmission: Kyan learned it in Tomari (Maeda Pēchin's line) and spread it to Seibukan, Matsubayashi-ryū and Isshin-ryū, while Itosu's students carried a version to Japan, where Funakoshi renamed it Empi in the mid-1930s. The Wang Ji story is folklore; the Tomari mainline is covered under the Tomari-te area.

name: Kanchin
meaning: Kanbun's battle (Kan from Kanbun/Kanei plus 'battle'). A memorial kata: Kanei assembled it from his father's favoured fighting techniques, making it a codified record of Kanbun Uechi's personal karate.
provenance: Authored by Kanei Uechi around 1960 as the penultimate kata of the eight, honouring Kanbun Uechi with aggressive stepping, shoken strikes and hip-driven pivots drawn from his father's practice.

name: Kanshiwa
meaning: A name built from the kanji of Kanbun Uechi (Kan) and Shu Shiwa (Shiwa): it honours the teacher-student bond that founded the style. First of the post-war bridging kata, teaching tiger-style strength to beginners.
provenance: One of five kata added by Kanei Uechi and his seniors after Kanbun's death (1948) to bridge the large gaps between the original three; lineage accounts credit its composition to the group around Kanei Uechi with Saburo Uehara, and it was initially called Kanshabu.

name: Kanshu
variants: Daini Seisan (second Seisan, early name); Kansu
meaning: Kanbun (Kan) plus Shu (Zhou, the surname of Shu Shiwa): a second homage to the founding lineage. A preparatory study for Seisan, hence its early name Daini Seisan.
provenance: Composed by Seiki Itokazu, a senior student of Kanei Uechi who later founded Konan-ryu (1978, with Takashi Kinjo); adopted into the standard eight-kata Uechi-ryu syllabus under Kanei's systematisation.

name: Sanseiryu
meaning: Thirty-six. The highest of the three original Pangai-noon kata, embodying the dragon: low simultaneous attack and defence, whipping open-hand strikes and coordinated whole-body power.
era: Qing-era China; learned by Kanbun Uechi c. 1897-1907
origin_person: Shu Shiwa (Zhou Zihe) (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
provenance: Kanbun Uechi reportedly spent his final years with Zhou Zihe mastering this kata alone; it remained the terminal kata when Kanei Uechi expanded the syllabus to eight. Distinct from the Goju/To'on/Ryuei Sanseiru despite the shared numeric name.

name: Seichin
variants: Seichin (also glossed 'ten battles' or as a Sanchin-Seisan blend)
meaning: Usually read as 'ten battles' (or as a contraction of Seisan plus Sanchin). Blends Sanchin tension with Seisan-like flowing movement and introduces the dragon element's soft whipping techniques.
provenance: Created in the mid-1950s by Saburo Uehara, patriarch of the Shubukai branch, under Kanei Uechi's direction as part of the post-war expansion of the syllabus to eight kata. [Verifier: Kata, meaning gloss ('ten battles' / Seisan+Sanchin contraction) and 1950s date are right. Wikipedia credits Saburo Uehara as creator, matching the entry, but Okikukai material says Seiki Itokazu headed the developmen

name: Seiryu
meaning: Sixteen (the kanji count; the reading also evokes 'blue dragon'). Introduces softer circular open-hand deflections, low sweeps and turning defences between Seisan and Kanchin.
provenance: One of Kanei Uechi's own compositions in the post-war expansion, developed around 1950 while he was building the Futenma dojo curriculum with the Tomoyose family's support.

name: Seisan (Uechi)
meaning: Thirteen. The middle kata of the original Pangai-noon three: tiger-style open-hand strikes, one-knuckle punches (shoken) and the signature jumping front-kick sequence.
era: Qing-era China; learned by Kanbun Uechi c. 1897-1907
origin_person: Shu Shiwa (Zhou Zihe) (transmitted; ultimate creator unknown)
provenance: A separate transmission from the Naha and Shuri Seisan lines: Kanbun Uechi learned it from Zhou Zihe (Shu Shiwa) in Fuzhou and taught it in Wakayama from 1926; his son Kanei fixed the modern form when he systematised the style after 1948.
